Odin × Godot

Building gameplay: the kit + play recipe

11 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Layer 1: an entity is a struct of play fieldsLayer 2: assigning authority and presentationWorked example: the fire / reload / jam gunResponsibilities across five gameplay itemsChecklist for a new itemSee also

A networked gameplay item has data, player intent, authority decisions, and presentation that may run on different peers or clocks. Kit represents its shared state in registered entities; the play package supplies local state machines, timing, and transition tracking. This recipe shows how to compose those pieces without mixing authority decisions into presentation.

The recipe first embeds reusable state in an entity, then assigns the work for an item to seven responsibilities: state, cadence, intent, authority, prediction, reconciliation, and presentation. A gun example shows all seven, and a table compares five gameplay items.

Several examples use an earlier Scrapyard implementation and the removed play.Machine, play.step, and play.set APIs. Those examples are retained as design references and cannot be copied into this checkout unchanged. Current blocks such as play.Gun use generated command reconciliation; see kit/play. Runner below names the game's character script.

The networking distinctions used here are:

  • Replicated fields retain shared state for updates and snapshots. Events represent occurrences that do not need the same persistence.
  • Commands ask the authority to validate a target mutation. Owner streams are a separate policy for fields whose values the game trusts the owner to write.
  • State updates arrive before delayed remote motion is necessarily displayed. Spatial effects need to follow the clock of their visible cause.

Layer 1: an entity is a struct of play fields#

An entity is a struct, and its behaviors are play primitives embedded as fields. From scrapyard, the co-op twin-stick example:

Odin
Runner :: struct {
    owner:  gd.Node2d,
    x, y:   f32 `gd:"owner,wire=f16"`, // continuous owner fields interpolate by default
    hp:     u8  `gd:"replicate"`,
    gun:    u8  `gd:"replicate"`,

    ammo:      u8 `gd:"replicate"`,       // rounds in the mag
    gun_fsm:   play.Machine(Gun_State),   // Ready / Reloading / Jammed — cur replicates
    reload_cd: u16 `gd:"replicate"`,      // host countdown to reload done

    rev_target: u32 `gd:"owner"`, // who I'm reviving
    rev_pct:    u8  `gd:"owner"`, // channel progress 0..255

    seen_hp: play.Edge(u8),               // local: damage-flash edge detector
}

The example groups gun state, damage transition tracking, and revive progress in Runner. Embedding a struct keeps that behavior's data together without adding another Godot node.

Scriptgen recursively includes tagged fields from embedded structs in the containing entity's wire descriptor. In the earlier play.Machine(Gun_State) example, cur: Gun_State \gd:"replicate"`was replicated as part ofRunner, while its untagged shadow` stayed local for presentation change tracking.

How these differ from Godot components:

  • The "components" are plain Odin sub-structs (data + free procs), not nodes. There is no tree, no get_node, and no per-instance allocation: they're fields, resolved at build time.
  • Their "signals" are edges, not engine signals: you read a play.Edge / play.step transition in the render path, rather than connecting a callback (see Pure-Odin Events for callbacks across systems).
  • They compose at the struct level, flattened by scriptgen, not at the scene-tree level at runtime.

Scriptgen carries an embedded block's wire, export, @onready, signal, and command declarations into the containing entity. A @(gd_command) whose receiver is the block gets an entry in the entity's command table. If its signature requests the containing entity, the generated call supplies that pointer, called the wielder. Nested blocks compose recursively, such as gun → loadout → character. The game still implements cross-entity consequences. See kit/ — composing verbs from embedded blocks.

Gameplay primitives#

These primitives have different execution requirements. Edge, Pace, anim, and the earlier Machine operate on Odin data. marker calls the engine for presentation; Puppet and Puppet3 drive engine physics. The last column lists each one's usual responsibility in the next section.

Primitive What it is Pure? Usually the…
play.Edge(T) A client-local shadow of a value; see reports the one frame it moved. ✅ Presentation trigger
play.Pace(T) A re-armable deadline; the earlier Deadlines(K,T) keyed several. ✅ Cadence gate
play.Machine(S) Earlier state machine with replicated cur; absent from this checkout. ✅ State (a mode)
play.anim Presentation float clocks: decay/ramp/advance/hold/pulse. ✅ Presentation rendering
play.marker Lazy world-markers: show/follow/fill/depth over a built node. ❌ engine Presentation rendering
play.Puppet The owner's RigidBody2D solver streams pose and velocity; other peers freeze the body and interpolate it. session_set_owner transfers control with velocity retained. ❌ engine State (a shared body)
play.Puppet3 RigidBody3D version with quaternion rotation through stream-layer .Quat nlerp, linear and angular velocity transfer, and positions in meters. The 2D version snaps rotation. ❌ engine State (a shared body)

Tags on a block's fields determine what replicates. The earlier Machine.cur used gd:"replicate"; current Puppet and Puppet3 fields carry owner-streamed pose and velocity. Edge, Pace, anim clocks, and marker handles are local scratch, stored in authority bookkeeping or a render-side view. Embedding a block includes the network tags it declares.

Layer 2: assigning authority and presentation#

After choosing the entity's fields, assign each operation to the process allowed to perform it. An item's work can span the client, authority, and presentation loop. The following seven responsibilities help identify where that work belongs:

# Slot The question it answers Lives on Filled by
1 State What's true on every screen? everyone (replicated) kit gd:"replicate"; play.Machine for a mode
2 Cadence When is it allowed to act? client gate + host play.Pace / Deadlines
3 Intent Which mutation does the client request? client → host @(gd_command)
4 Authority Who decides, and what decays each tick? host only the command hook + host_*_tick
5 Prediction Which result can be computed before a reply? client the predict command body
6 Reconcile How is the local result updated from authority state? client this example's view adopts host transitions; generated commands use built-in reconciliation
7 Presentation How does it read, once per change, on every screen? everyone play.Edge/step → anim/marker

Use only the responsibilities the item needs. An authority-controlled pickup can need State, Authority, and Presentation without a player-issued Intent. The mob example similarly needs no local Prediction or Reconcile. The matrix compares the work required by each item.

Prediction provides a local response before an authority result arrives. Reconciliation applies accepted state when the local result differs. The gun example shows how those operations affect cadence and presentation.

Worked example: the fire / reload / jam gun#

The gun uses all seven responsibilities. An empty magazine moves it from Ready → (fire) → Reloading; a dud moves it from Ready → Jammed, and repeated trigger pulls clear the jam. The host accepts gameplay results. The client predicts eligible transitions before receiving authority updates.

Current reusable blocks include play.Gun for magazine, reload, and jam state; play.Ability for a cooldown cast; and play.Channel for a hold-to-progress action such as revive. Their tagged command mutations use kit/net's built-in prediction and reconciliation. The earlier manual example below separates these responsibilities for explanation. See composing verbs from embedded blocks.

The following excerpts show each responsibility with surrounding game code omitted.

1. State is the minimum every screen needs to render the HUD and let the host gate:

Odin
ammo:      u8 `gd:"replicate"`,
gun_fsm:   play.Machine(Gun_State),   // cur ∈ {Ready, Reloading, Jammed}, replicated
reload_cd: u16 `gd:"replicate"`,      // ticks left on the reload dwell
jam_taps:  u8,                        // host-only scratch — never replicated

2. Cadence uses one local clock for fire cooldown, reload duration, and jam-clear attempts. Check the deadline before issuing the next command:

Odin
if !play.due(&self.next_shot, now) { return false }
cd := gun_cooldown(r.gun, r.boost_rate, r.parts)
play.arm(&self.next_shot, now + f64(cd + 1) / hz)   // +1 tick of grace over the host's gate

3. Intent requests a target mutation. A predicted command runs the same procedure locally on the client and authoritatively on the host:

Odin
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_OWNER_PREDICTED)
runner_fire :: proc(self: ^Runner, dx, dy, ox, oy: f32) -> bool { ... }

4. Authority accepts the fire, jam, or clear result in the command hook. The per-tick host_*_tick advances the reload countdown. The play.set calls in these earlier excerpts update accepted state on the host:

Odin
// in the command hook — the host's verdict on this pull:
switch r.gun_fsm.cur {
case .Reloading: return                       // a shot that raced the reload — dropped
case .Jammed:
    if r.jam_taps > 0 { r.jam_taps -= 1 }
    if r.jam_taps == 0 { play.set(&r.gun_fsm, Gun_State.Ready) }
    return
case .Ready:
    if jam_roll(player, r.ammo, floor, r.gun) {
        r.ammo -= 1; play.set(&r.gun_fsm, Gun_State.Jammed); r.jam_taps = JAM_TAPS
        return
    }
    r.ammo -= 1
    if r.ammo == 0 { play.set(&r.gun_fsm, Gun_State.Reloading); r.reload_cd = gun_reload_ticks(r.gun) }
    // ... spawn the authoritative damaging projectile ...
}

// in host_combat_tick — the authoritative half of the reload dwell:
if r.gun_fsm.cur == .Reloading && r.reload_cd > 0 {
    r.reload_cd -= 1
    if r.reload_cd == 0 { r.ammo = gun_mag(r.gun); play.set(&r.gun_fsm, Gun_State.Ready) }
}

5. Prediction computes a local result before the network round trip. The jam calculation is deterministic: equal player, ammo, floor, and gun values produce the same roll. The prediction can still differ if the client has stale state; the host's result remains authoritative.

Odin
// runner.odin — equal inputs on client and host produce the same result:
jam_roll :: proc "contextless" (player: knet.Player_Id, ammo, floor, gun: u8) -> bool {
    if g_no_jam { return false }
    h := u32(player)*2654435761 + u32(ammo)*40503 + u32(floor)*2246822519 + u32(gun)*668265263
    h ~= h>>15; h *= 2246822519; h ~= h>>13
    thresh := gun == GUN_RIVETER ? u32(30) : u32(12)   // 3% / 1.2% per shot
    return (h % 1000) < thresh
}

The client predicts fire, ammo consumption, and jams locally. It also holds the pacer through the predicted reload duration.

6. Reconcile updates this example's separate client gun view when the host's mode changes. It adopts the opening magazine once, then copies the mode and ammo at a transition. This is a view-specific policy, not a replacement for generated command reconciliation.

Odin
gun_reconcile :: proc(self: ^Scrapyard, r: ^Runner) {
    if !self.gun_init { /* adopt the host's opening mag once */ ... return }
    if _, moved := play.see(&self.gun_seen, r.gun_fsm.cur); moved {
        self.gun_state = r.gun_fsm.cur   // a reload finished / a jam landed or cleared
        self.gun_ammo  = r.ammo
    }
}

7. Presentation reacts to changes in the replicated cur. In this earlier example, play.step reports the transition for effects without accepting gameplay results:

Odin
gun_edges :: proc(self: ^Scrapyard) {
    for id, r in self.runners {
        _, to, moved := play.step(&r.gun_fsm)
        if !moved { continue }
        #partial switch to {
        case .Jammed: kfx.burst_at(...); kfx.float_text(..., "JAM"); kfx.flash(...)
        case .Ready:  kfx.burst_at(..., {0.5, 0.95, 0.55, 1})   // a small confirming pop
        }
    }
}

The host reads the state it set, and clients read the state received through replication. Each runs the transition check locally. Effects therefore follow observed state changes rather than a separate RPC for each effect. Changes that begin and end between comparisons can coalesce; use occurrence events when each instance must be presented.

Responsibilities across five gameplay items#

The gun uses all seven responsibilities. The five earlier Scrapyard items below show which work each item requires; an empty cell means that example needs no separate implementation for that responsibility.

Slot Gun Revive (channel) Mob brain Match phase Pickup
State gun_fsm, ammo, reload_cd rev_target, rev_pct, hp mob x/y/hp world.stage (Machine) scrap entities
Cadence next_shot (Pace f64) channel ramp next_act/next_add (Pace u64) over_at (Pace) —
Intent runner_fire (predict) runner_revive (plain) — — —
Authority fire hook + tick dwell host_honor_revive the *_brain procs play.set sites proximity scan
Prediction try_fire + jam_roll — — — —
Reconcile gun_reconcile — — — —
Presentation gun_edges (step) revive-bar marker telegraph + logs step → banner despawn

Revive: a channeled ability. A plain (non-predicted) command: runner_revive only asserts the target is down; host_honor_revive re-checks kinter.in_range and the reviver's pulse before granting hp. This example does not predict the result because reach depends on another player's authoritative state. Each peer renders the channel bar from rev_pct, building it once and updating it with play.marker:

Odin
play.show(self.revive_bar, active)
play.follow(self.revive_bar, d.x, d.y - 44)
play.fill(cast(gd.Node2d)self.revive_fill, f32(pct) / 255)   // each peer renders the bar

Mob brain: a host-only actor. This example needs Cadence, Authority, State, and Presentation. One host procedure drives its behavior, with no player Intent or local Prediction and Reconcile. Its timers group Pace values on the network tick in the style of play.Deadlines:

Odin
Mob_Brain :: struct {
    next_act: play.Pace(u64),   // next bite / spit / slam tick
    next_add: play.Pace(u64),   // boss only: next add-spawn tick
}
// in boss_brain:
if play.due(&m.brain.next_act, s.tick) && s.dist <= reach { m.tele = SLAM_WIND; return }
if frac <= BOSS_ADDS_AT && play.due(&m.brain.next_add, s.tick) {
    play.arm(&m.brain.next_add, s.tick + BOSS_ADD_CD); spawn_adds()
}

Match phase: a singleton Machine. In the earlier example, world.stage is a play.Machine(u8) on the world/session singleton; the host drives it through play.set (lobby → fight → clear → over), and every system reads w.stage.cur to gate what it does. There is no per-player Intent, Prediction, or Reconcile. This is the same Machine used by the gun, stored on the singleton instead of the character:

Odin
if from, to, moved := play.step(&w.stage); moved { /* trace / banner the phase change */ }
if all_runners_down(self) { play.set(&w.stage, STAGE_OVER); play.arm(&self.over_at, now_s() + 2.5) }

Pickup: an ambient world rule. No command at all: the host scans proximity each tick, credits the stat, and despawns the entity. It needs Authority, State, and Presentation. The client displays the updated scrap counter:

Odin
reach := PICKUP_R + (part_has(r.parts, PART_MAGNET) ? MAGNET_REACH : 0)
if dist2(sc.x, sc.y, r.x, r.y) <= reach*reach {
    ksess.session_stat_add(&self.ses, pid, self.scrap_col, i64(sc.amount)); append(&picked, id)
}

Contact attack. A bite, maul, or touch attack can combine a play.Pace in the attacker's authority bookkeeping, a range check, and play.health_hurt on the victim. There is no play.Melee block; these operations express the attack directly.

Odin
// in the attacker's host brain (bite_cd: play.Pace(u64) rides the brain scratch):
if dist2(m.x, m.y, prey.x, prey.y) <= reach*reach && play.ready(&m.brain.bite_cd, tick, BITE_CD) {
    play.health_hurt(&prey.health, BITE_DMG)
}

Authority position history. The interpolation buffer retains received samples for rendering. Mechanics such as hitscan judgment, recall, or a death recap may also need history recorded by the authority. The earlier Scrapyard lance used ping/2 + interp delay to select a past mob position. A fixed ring in host scratch can store one position per tick and select an entry by modulo index at query time. Unwritten slots need a sentinel or validity flag; test a mob at its live position when it is younger than the history window:

Odin
Mob_Brain :: struct { hist: [30][2]f32, ... }        // 30 ticks = 500ms at 60Hz
m.brain.hist[tick % 30] = {m.x, m.y}                 // top of the host tick loop
h := m.brain.hist[(tick - rewind) % 30]              // the query — clamp rewind to the window

This example uses an inline ring because the window, value type, and process recording it depend on the mechanic.

Checklist for a new item#

For each item, identify the state, cadence, request, authority result, prediction, reconciliation, and presentation work it needs:

  1. State: replicate the values peers need. The earlier play.Machine grouped a replicated cur tagged gd:"replicate" with a local change shadow. In current code, represent modes with explicit state fields and use generated field edges for replicated transitions. Keep Edge, Pace, timers, and presentation clocks local unless deliberately included in network state.

  2. Prediction: predict results that are deterministic from shared inputs. Cooldowns and jam_roll can qualify. An AOE that mutates many entities, or a check against another player's authoritative state, stays host-only in these examples, such as revive and slime. A plain command avoids showing speculative success when the client cannot make a reliable local check.

  3. Cadence: use the local pacer to schedule eligible attempts while the host validates them. The example issues fire through play.due(&next_shot, ...) rather than waiting for a received gun_fsm.cur to become Ready. This avoids adding a network wait to each local attempt.

  4. Reconciliation: generated predicted commands apply authority updates and replay pending commands. For the separate gun view shown above, play.see detects mode transitions before adopting cur and ammo. Keep this view policy separate from the runtime's correction of replicated entity state.

  5. Presentation: read transitions to show effects without accepting gameplay results. The earlier example used play.step; play.Edge remains useful for local or derived state. After snapshot catch-up, call play.sync on manually maintained shadows so a prior wound does not look like a fresh hit. Generated field edges handle their own baseline seeding.

Record which of the seven responsibilities the item needs, which process performs each one, and which state or event carries its result to other peers.

See also#

  • kit/ overview: the per-package reference for the systems the Intent and Authority slots are built on (session, combat, interact, net, …).
  • Pure-Odin Events: one-to-many callback dispatch across systems instead of a per-frame edge read.
  • The play/ source: current primitives are documented at their definitions (play/edge.odin, pace.odin, anim.odin, marker.odin). The earlier fsm.odin reference belongs to the historical examples; that file is absent from this checkout. Use the current source comments for API details.
